text.p: President Bill Clinton spoke at a $500,000 fund-raiser for the Democratic National Committee on Monday evening, continuing to drum up cash for his party despite questions about its money-raising practices.

But Clinton didn't mention the controversy to the 75 members of the Democratic Business Council, a branch of the DNC, who paid either $10,000 in individual, or $15,000 in corporate or PAC contributions, to join the group and eat grilled beef, Duchesse potatoes and creme brulee at the elegant Sheraton Carlton hotel event.
After extolling the economy and his administration's achievements, Clinton said the group must help ensure the success of welfare reform by hiring recipients off the roles.
"We have to set an example, we can't just exhort people," Clinton said. "We changed the law, now we have to do our part."
He also urged the contributors to help the campaign of Democratic Sen. Barbara Boxer of California, who was at the dinner, and who could face a tough fight next year to retain her seat.

Several prominent Democrats, including Wisconsin Sen. Russell Feingold, over the weekend called for the appointment of an independent counsel to investigate the fund raising practices of both parties during the 1996 election.
Feingold is a co-sponsor of legislation that Clinton backs to reform the campaign finance system.
Clinton earlier described the current furore over campaign financing as "hand wringing."

"You know, we're all in a lather up here in Washington these days about campaign contributions; everybody hates them, but nobody wants to go to public funding," Clinton said in a speech to educators. "So we seem destined to some period of hand-wringing."

The White House on Monday reiterated that it would not comment on whether an independent counsel should be named, referring queries to the Justice Department, which is responsible for such appointments.
"The Justice Department makes determinations based on the evidence on that matter. I don't have any comment for you," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.

McCurry defended Clinton's attending Monday's fund-raiser, noting that the Republican Party continues to raise money and that, under the current system, the parties have little choice but to finance their activities through such donations.

"The president will continue, as we've said over and over again, to help the party raise money. They need the money," McCurry said. "They need to be competitive with the Republican Party. As you've noticed, the Republican Party has been actively and aggressively raising money of their own."
